title: Op-ed | The Children We Cannot Afford to Overlook
content:
Conflict and humanitarian crises have devastating consequences for healthcare systems, often leaving children without access to essential medical treatment. Yet the need for surgical care does not disappear when international attention shifts elsewhere. In this piece, Yusra Mardini and Sarah Masiyiwa explore why children’s surgical care must be a priority in humanitarian responses and long-term recovery.

In December 2024, the fall of the Assad regime, after nearly 14 years of devastating civil war, brought hope to many Syrians. But the end of a regime does not mean the end of a country’s suffering. When Yusra returned to Syria in 2025, ten years after being forced to leave her home, she found a country both familiar and profoundly changed. Beyond the physical destruction lay the enormous challenge of rebuilding the services and institutions people depend on every day.

Among them is surgical care for children.

title: The Killers of Journalists Are Getting Away with Murder. Governments Must Act to End Impunity.
content:
On the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes Against Journalists, IFEX exposes the gulf between governments’ commitments to media freedom and their failure to deliver justice. From the unprecedented number of journalists killed in Gaza to the question of who ordered the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta, those responsible continue to evade accountability. Meanwhile, civil society organisations and international institutions pursuing accountability face growing pressure.

The murder of a journalist is rarely an isolated crime. It is an attempt to suppress information, obstruct scrutiny and deny the public the truth. When perpetrators escape justice, sources are silenced, colleagues are intimidated and those who abuse power emboldened.

More than 100 IFEX member organisations document attacks, support journalists at risk and demand accountability. The scale of the crisis is stark: nine in ten cases involving the killings of journalists and media workers go unpunished.[1] In 2025, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) recorded 129 journalists and media workers killed, the highest annual toll since the organisation’s records began in 1992.[2]

title: Op-ed | What the US Midterms Could Mean for American Foreign Policy
content:
On 3 November, the United States (US) will hold midterm elections. Polls point towards a result which will change the balance of power in Washington, with the Democratic Party predicted to take control of the House of Representatives and quite possibly the Senate. Even just a Democratic victory in the House – the lower chamber of Congress – could have implications for American foreign policy.

These implications could push in two contradictory directions. On the one hand, Congress has some powers which are relevant to US foreign policy. The Senate – the upper house of Congress – must give its consent to treaties and ambassadorial appointments. Congress as a whole must approve the budget for the US military and for the country’s diplomatic agencies. It also has the power to investigate and hold to account officials who engage in corrupt or lawless behaviour. All of this suggests that a Democratic Congress could impose meaningful restraints on President Donald Trump.

title: Op-ed | The UK’S Long and Winding Road Back to Brussels
content: Andy Burnham’s recent party conference speech marked a fundamental shift in the UK’s position on a future relationship with the European Union, effectively abandoning the post-Brexit ‘red lines’ set out in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto. The four options mentioned by the Prime Minister are preserving the status quo, joining a customs union, joining the single market, or full EU membership (‘going all the way’). The 2024 manifesto had explicitly ruled out returning to the customs union or the single market or allowing freedom of movement. Beyond acknowledging that Brexit has done ‘more harm than good’, Burnham has so far given no indication of his preferred option.

title: Op-ed | Conflict Prevention Has Never Been More Important
content:
To mark the International Day of Peace (21 September), Alex Ballinger MP and Alastair Carr draw on Peace Works – a new report from a coalition of peacebuilding organisations – to argue that a more dangerous world requires the UK to protect the capacity to prevent conflict as well as respond to it.

In July 2011, the UK Government published its Building Stability Overseas Strategy, outlining three guiding principles for conflict prevention: early warning, rapid response and upstream prevention.[1]

Fifteen years on, these principles endure, but the world they were written for is gone. The institutions and assumptions of the liberal international order have weakened and fragmented, replaced by unilateralism, ad hoc alliances, and the arbitrary exercise of hard power.

title: Long Read | The State of the UN
content:
As the international order becomes increasingly fragmented, the United Nations appears weaker than it has for decades. But what has actually been lost, and what does the UN still provide that states cannot easily replace? Ahead of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Fred Carver examines what a weakened UN means for the UK and where the new Government should invest its political capital.

The United Nations (UN) is not in good shape, but it is worth considering a little more carefully what precisely it is that is not working, and what actually still is.

The UN delivers an extraordinary amount of development and humanitarian work. For a long time the organisation leaned into this aspect of its work because it showed tangible results.Yet commendable as much of this work is,  it was not an irreplaceable function, and perhaps others are far better placed to deliver it. Donors, Trump foremost among them, are now demanding a drastic and rapid downgrading of this capability, resulting in much short-term pain and waste.

title: Long Read | Immigration Policy: The Backdoor to Transnational Repression
content:
Did the United States (US) help Iran track down its own dissidents?

On 7 July, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund (IALDF) filed a lawsuit alleging exactly that. The Complaint alleges US immigration authorities shared confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government to facilitate their removal from the United States. If substantiated, the allegations reveal more than an extraordinary instance of cooperation between geopolitical adversaries. They suggest that the US immigration system may have become a vehicle for transnational repression, enabling an authoritarian regime to reach dissidents beyond its borders.

As such, the case exposes a broader paradox: democratic governments present themselves as committed to countering transnational repression, yet their increasingly restrictive migration policies may be helping autocrats achieve precisely what those efforts seek to prevent.

title: Op-ed | A Camel Called the Investor Visa
content:
The UK Government is reportedly considering the reintroduction of an investor visa for high-net-worth individuals. In this op-ed, Matthew McGlynn examines the economic, security and anti-corruption implications of reviving a scheme that was closed in 2022.

There is an old line that a camel is a horse designed by committee. The Starmer Government reported plans to revive an investor visa – invite-only, £5 million minimum, enhanced vetting, a three-year path to settlement – are the embodied camel.[1] The scheme is too narrow and too expensive to compete with its international counterparts, but also too toxic for a country still trying to shake off its ‘Londongrad’moniker. The Burnham Government would do well to simply scrap this idea.

title: Beyond the Ballot Box: Democracy Is What Happens Between Elections
content:
Democracy, for me, means accountable institutions anchored in the rule of law. It is not just about elections. Rather, it is everything that happens between elections to ensure people have access to three core values: dignity, safety, and a sense of belonging to a healthy and free society.

Moldova is experiencing the ruptures in the international rules-based order deeply. As Ukraine’s neighbour, we are close to the frontline of its efforts to defend its sovereignty and European security. From the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion, we have faced threats to our own security, concerted efforts to undermine our democratic institutions, and a huge influx of refugees.[1]

Moldova is a small country of 2.6 million people, yet in the first months of the war we hosted nearly one million Ukrainian refugees. Our society has not fractured – and Moldovan civil society has been instrumental in sustaining that cohesion, working alongside government and international partners.

title: Resistance Is Not Enough: Rethinking the Belarusian Democratic Movement
content:
A turning point is approaching for the Belarusian Democratic Forces, which emerged in response to the rigged presidential elections in 2020. They have begun to lose momentum after six years of tireless advocacy for democratic change – and it is time for the movement to have a serious conversation about its current shape and strategic direction.

Negotiations between the US and Belarusian authorities, which resulted in the release of hundreds of political prisoners, have deepened divisions within the movement into two opposing camps: the supporters of the hard-pressure approach that allows no compromise until the regime is defeated, and the proponents of a flexible approach that accepts limited concessions as a means of securing incremental gains. This dilemma revealed much more than differences in tactics. It exposed a rupture around the fundamental question: what kind of political actor must the democratic movement become if it is to reclaim Belarus? Every geopolitical shift — negotiations over prisoners, the end of the war in Ukraine, changing Western priorities — will only deepen the divisions and further delay the prospect of returning home.
